details:
What does it do and how does it work?

N.A.C.H.O. (NASA Administration Crew Health Onboard) is a prototype biomedical monitor for crews on space missions. It has three parts working together: sensors designed by the team to capture each crew member's vital signs, a monitor that analyzes those signs, and a guide that tells the crew what to do.

The monitor displays the electrocardiogram, pulse wave, respiration, mean arterial pressure, oxygen saturation and temperature of four crew members in real time. It also turns the spaceflight risks studied by NASA into measurable indicators: bone density loss by body region, radiation with a Geiger counter and likely symptoms by dose, spine health, immunity, venous flow, spinal fluid biomarkers, intracranial pressure, SANS and stress level.

When it detects a problem, it opens a window in front of the monitor with numbered instructions in plain language: put on oxygen, breathe along with a counter, give chest compressions at the right pace, or use the defibrillator only if the heart rhythm allows it. If the case is serious, it sounds an alert for the whole crew. When there is no emergency, it occasionally suggests short wellbeing activities (guided breathing, journaling, plant care, Earth gazing) to counter isolation and confinement.

Benefits

- The crew detects problems early, before they become serious.

- Astronauts, who are not doctors, know what to do step by step without waiting for Earth.

- Silent risks (bone, radiation, stress) become visible and measurable.

- It looks after mental health as well as physical health.

Intended impact

On missions to the Moon or Mars, communication with Earth can take up to about 20 minutes each way and a doctor will not always be on board. N.A.C.H.O. aims to make the crew more autonomous in caring for its own health. The same idea could help on Earth in isolated places such as Antarctic stations, offshore platforms or rural communities without a doctor.

Tools, languages and hardware

- Python 3 with tkinter for the monitor, with no external libraries.

- ESP32 TTGO T-Display board programmed with ESPHome for the sensor module.

- Public NASA information (Human Research Program) and studies on stress in spaceflight as the basis for the indicators.

- Git and GitHub for the code.

- Artificial intelligence tools as support for coding and writing.

At this stage the sensor and monitor data are simulated.

Why is it creative?

It is not just a monitor that shows numbers: it translates each alarm into concrete actions for people without medical training, includes an animated counter for breathing or chest compressions, and tells whether a cardiac arrest is shockable or not. It also brings immediate health, long-term spaceflight risks and emotional wellbeing together on a single screen.

Factors the team considered

- Astronauts are not doctors: short sentences, one action per step, no technical terms.

- Communication delay: the system works on board, without depending on Earth.

- Making everything measurable, based on what NASA studies.

- A screen that reads quickly in an emergency: colors by alarm level and large text.

- The limits of the prototype: the data is simulated, the formulas are approximations and the guides must be validated by medical staff before any real use.
